_comment: SIZE x DATA on the SAME-RULE rung: the only place a scaling law can
actually be measured.
Why this and not more of the new-rule rung. The new-rule size axis came back
flat at chance across 6.5x parameters, which rules out 'a bigger model would
have induced the rule'. It says nothing about the rung where transfer is
KNOWN to exist: subst-fst-fixed holds one substitution map constant, and
held-out byte there rises 0.329 -> 0.850 as training data grows 16 -> 288 at
a single model size. That is a curve, not a law. A law needs the curve at
more than one size, which is what this manifest makes reachable.
Run the DATA axis at each size (the sweep tool varies one axis per call):
for d in 128 192 384; do
cargo run --example scaling_sweep -- \
research/experiments/same-rule-size.json data gpu 16 48 128 288 \
--seeds=0,1,2   # with .model.d_model overridden to $d
done
The sweep's `params` axis sets d_model and derives n_heads, so the simpler
route is one call per size using the axis tool directly and reading the data
cap from this manifest. Either way the invariant that matters: the eval set
must be IDENTICAL at every point, which the data axis guarantees by capping
AFTER the holdout.
WHY THIS IS WORTH THE GPU TIME. Every other axis in this repo has produced a
null or an unresolved single pass. This one has produced the only non-null,
monotone, multi-point curve in the project -- 0.329 to 0.850 across an 18x
data range. A second and third size on that curve turns it into the scaling
result the goal actually asks for. If the slopes differ by size, that is the
finding; if they do not, that is also the finding, and it is a much cheaper
one to have established than a 6.5x null on the other rung.
Read with off_pair_rate as well as byte accuracy. On this rung byte accuracy
is well clear of chance (0.85+), so it is the informative column; off_pair
additionally tells you whether the model is transferring the rule or
producing plausible in-alphabet output, which byte accuracy alone cannot
separate.
k_set is [0]: the rule is in the weights, and demos would only add context
length. Same reasoning as data-axis-constant-rule.json, which this extends.
